chapter_title: Static Timing Analysis and Timing Constraints
chapter_summary:
Static Timing Analysis (STA) is the method used to verify that a digital circuit meets its timing requirements without simulating the design. Unlike dynamic simulation, which checks logic behavior, STA mathematically analyzes every possible path in the circuit to ensure that signals arrive at flip-flops before the setup time and remain stable through the hold time. STA is exhaustive: it checks every path, not just the ones exercised by a testbench. This makes it the gold standard for timing verification in both FPGA and ASIC design.

The fundamental timing equation for a synchronous circuit is:

```
T_clock >= T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew
```

Where:
- **T_clock:** The clock period (time between clock edges). For a 50 MHz clock, T_clock = 20 ns.
- **T_co (Clock-to-Q delay):** The time from the clock edge to when the flip-flop output becomes stable. For a typical FPGA flip-flop, T_co is about 0.2 ns.
- **T_logic (Propagation delay):** The time for a signal to travel through the combinational logic between flip-flops. This is the sum of LUT delays, routing delays, and carry chain delays.
- **T_setup (Setup time):** The minimum time the data input must be stable before the clock edge. For a typical FPGA flip-flop, T_setup is about 0.1 ns.
- **T_skew (Clock skew):** The difference in arrival time of the clock at different flip-flops. Clock skew is caused by unequal wire lengths in the clock distribution network. It can be positive or negative.

If the total delay (T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew) is less than the clock period, the design meets setup time. If it is greater, the design has a **setup time violation**, which means the flip-flop may capture an incorrect value.

**Hold time** is the minimum time the data input must remain stable after the clock edge. A hold time violation occurs when the new data arrives too quickly after the clock edge, before the flip-flop has finished capturing the old data. Hold time violations are less common in FPGAs because the routing delay between flip-flops is usually long enough, but they can occur in designs with clock skew or when using the same clock edge for launch and capture.

**Timing constraints** are directives that tell the timing analyzer what the design requirements are. Without constraints, the tool cannot verify timing because it does not know the clock frequency or the expected input/output delays. Constraints are written in the **Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)** format, which is an industry standard supported by Quartus Prime, Vivado, and other tools.

The most important SDC command is `create_clock`, which defines the clock frequency and name:

```sdc
create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 [get_ports {clk}]
```

This defines a 50 MHz clock (20 ns period) on the port named `clk`. You can also add duty cycle, offset, and uncertainty:

```sdc
create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 -waveform {0.000 10.000} [get_ports {clk}]
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.200 [get_clocks {clk}]
```

Input delays are defined with `set_input_delay`:

```sdc
set_input_delay -clock {clk} -max 5.000 [get_ports {data_in}]
set_input_delay -clock {clk} -min 1.000 [get_ports {data_in}]
```

This tells the timing analyzer that the external device driving `data_in` provides it at most 5 ns after the clock edge and at least 1 ns after the clock edge. The FPGA must capture the data within the remaining window.

Output delays are defined with `set_output_delay`:

```sdc
set_output_delay -clock {clk} -max 3.000 [get_ports {data_out}]
```

This tells the timing analyzer that the external device requires `data_out` to be stable at least 3 ns before the next clock edge.

**False paths** and **multicycle paths** are also specified in the SDC file:
- A **false path** is a path that is never exercised in the design (e.g., a reset signal that is only active at power-up). You tell the tool to ignore it with `set_false_path`.
- A **multicycle path** is a path where the data is allowed to take multiple clock cycles (e.g., a slow divider output). You tell the tool with `set_multicycle_path`.

In Quartus Prime, the **TimeQuest Timing Analyzer** reads the SDC file and generates detailed timing reports. The key report is the **Setup Summary**, which shows the worst-case setup slack for each clock domain. Slack is the difference between the required time and the actual arrival time. Positive slack means the design meets timing; negative slack means it fails.

```
Setup Slack = Data Required Time - Data Arrival Time
```

If the slack is negative, the tool reports the **critical path** — the longest path from a launch flip-flop to a capture flip-flop. You can view the critical path in the TimeQuest GUI or in the timing report file. The critical path shows every node along the path: the launching flip-flop, the combinational logic (LUTs, carry chains), the routing delays, and the capturing flip-flop.

screens.title: Static Timing Analysis and Timing Constraints
screens.subtitle: Why timing matters, and how constraints make timing verification possible

narration.text: Static Timing Analysis, or STA, is the formal way we ensure a synchronous digital design meets its timing requirements without running exhaustive dynamic simulations. In practice, you will use STA to check every path a signal could take from a launching flip-flop to a capturing flip-flop, ensuring data meets setup and hold requirements under all conditions. This matters because simulation only exercises selected scenarios, while STA is exhaustive and finds worst-case timing paths that a testbench might miss. For example, when targeting a 50 megahertz clock, you must ensure the sum of clock-to-Q delay, logic propagation, setup time, and any clock skew fits inside the 20 nanosecond clock period. In this chapter you will learn the key timing terms, how to express constraints in Synopsys Design Constraints format — create_clock, input and output delays, false and multicycle paths — and how to read the TimeQuest or Vivado timing reports to find slack and the critical path. By the end, you will be able to write a basic. sdc file for a Quartus Prime project, interpret a Setup Summary, and reason about whether to add registers to pipeline long paths. Think about a design you can test: we'll use a 4-bit ALU as a working example to show how a pipeline stage changes maximum frequency and latency.

keyIdea.title: Why STA first?
keyIdea.text: STA checks every timing path exhaustively and lets synthesis tools guarantee timing without slow, incomplete simulations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain and how you'll apply them

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why Static Timing Analysis is used instead of relying only on dynamic simulation. You will define and measure key timing parameters: setup time and hold time for flip-flops, clock-to-Q delay, and the components of propagation delay through LUTs and routing. You will also be able to write basic Synopsys Design Constraints: create_clock entries for clock domains, set_input_delay and set_output_delay for input and output timing, and marks for false and multicycle paths. Finally, you will read timing reports from TimeQuest or Vivado, find the worst slack and the critical path, and reason about how adding registers can increase maximum clock frequency at the cost of latency. These objectives matter because they let you turn a functional RTL design into a timing-clean implementation ready for FPGA place-and-route, and because a single missed path can cause intermittent functional failure. To verify mastery, you will add a 50 megahertz clock constraint to a simple 4-bit ALU, run timing analysis, then increase the frequency and observe how slack and the critical path change.

keyIdea.text: You will move from theory to practice: write SDC constraints, run TimeQuest, and interpret slack and critical path reports.

screens.title: What is Static Timing Analysis (STA)?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role, and contrast with dynamic simulation

narration.text: Static Timing Analysis is a mathematical method that verifies timing constraints for synchronous digital circuits by examining every possible timing path between sequential elements, rather than by running time-based functional tests. In other words, STA looks at launch points and capture points, sums the delays along combinational paths, compares the result to the clock period and setup requirements, and reports slack. A clear practical example: if you have two flip-flops connected by a network of LUTs and routing, STA will compute the worst-case arrival time from the launching flip-flop's clock edge through clock-to-Q delay, logic and routing delays, and check it against the required setup window at the capturing flip-flop. Contrast this with dynamic simulation: a testbench can only exercise selected input patterns and may miss a corner-case timing path. A common misconception is to think simulation alone is sufficient; it is not. Simulation validates functionality but is not exhaustive for timing. STA is the gold standard because it is exhaustive and finds the true critical path even when a test vector never exercises it. Keep in mind STA depends on accurate timing models for flip-flops, LUTs, routing, and clock distribution provided by the FPGA vendor and on correct constraints to tell the tool the clock periods and input and output timing. The takeaway: use STA to guarantee timing closure, and use simulation to verify logical correctness.

keyIdea.title: STA vs Simulation
keyIdea.text: STA is exhaustive path-based timing verification; simulation verifies logic on exercised input vectors.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › STA Overview
Definition
STA analyzes every path mathematically to verify that signals meet timing constraints without dynamic event simulation.
Why use STA: exhaustive analysis finds worst-case paths that simulations may miss.
Dependency: accurate vendor timing libraries and correct constraints are required.
Common misconception: passing simulation does not guarantee timing closure.
Concrete example
Consider a register launching data through several LUTs to a capturing register on the next clock edge. STA computes the maximum arrival time and compares it to the required setup time for the capture register to determine slack.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

STA guarantees timing by analyzing all paths; use it with correct SDC constraints to trust timing reports.

Misconception
Assuming functional simulation proves timing. It does not; it is complementary.
Pro tip
Provide explicit clocks and I/O delays in SDC before running STA so the analyzer finds meaningful slack values.
Check
Always inspect the critical path reported by the tool to confirm the reason for negative slack.

screens.title: The Fundamental Timing Equation
screens.subtitle: How the clock period limits path timing and where slack comes from

narration.text: The central timing inequality for synchronous circuits guides all our timing checks. It states that the clock period must be at least the sum of the clock-to-Q delay, the combinational logic propagation delay, the setup time at the receiving flip-flop, plus any clock skew. Written plainly: the clock period must be greater than or equal to T_co plus T_logic plus T_setup plus T_skew. A concrete example uses a 50 megahertz clock where the period is 20 nanoseconds: if T_co is about 0.2 nanoseconds, T_setup about 0.1 nanoseconds, and the logic and routing sum to 15 nanoseconds with negligible skew, you have comfortable slack because 0.2 + 15 + 0.1 is less than 20. Slack is computed as Data Required Time minus Data Arrival Time; positive slack means timing passes, negative slack means violation. A typical misconception is to forget skew or to treat T_co as zero; neither is safe. Clock skew can be positive or negative and changes the required or available window. Practically, when a timing tool reports negative slack, it also identifies the critical path: the path whose arrival time most exceeds the required time. That path lists the launch register, each logic element, routing contributions, and the capture register, so you can decide whether to optimize logic, reduce routing, or insert a pipeline register. A guided question: if the worst-case sum of delays changes, how will slack and maximum clock frequency change? Use the equation to reason before editing RTL.

keyIdea.title: Timing inequality
keyIdea.text: T_clock must exceed T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew; slack measures the margin between required and actual arrival.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Timing Equation
The equation
T_clock ≥ T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew
Components explained
  • T_co — clock-to-Q delay of the launching flip-flop.
  • T_logic — combinational propagation through LUTs and routing.
  • T_setup — data stable before the capture clock edge.
  • T_skew — clock arrival differences between registers.
Slack = Data Required Time − Data Arrival Time
Worked example
Target clock: 50 MHz → T_clock = 20 ns. If T_co = 0.2 ns, T_setup = 0.1 ns and T_logic = 15 ns, then required = 0.2 + 15 + 0.1 = 15.3 ns. Slack = 20 − 15.3 = 4.7 ns (positive).
Check your thinking
Try this

If a path reports −2 ns slack, what must you change: reduce T_logic, reduce skew, or increase T_clock? Consider which is feasible for your design.

Misconception
Treating T_co as negligible. Even small flip-flop delays matter when pushing frequency.
Pro tip
Estimate worst-case path with the equation before running timing tools to guide where to optimize.
Why it matters
The equation directly gives maximum clock frequency and informs pipelining decisions.

screens.title: Flip-flop timing: T_co, T_setup, and hold time
screens.subtitle: Precise meanings and why each matters

narration.text: Flip-flop timing parameters are fundamental to STA. Clock-to-Q delay, or T_co, is the time from the triggering clock edge until the flip-flop's output is stable. Setup time is the minimum interval before the clock edge that data must be stable at the data input; it ensures the capture latch samples the correct value. Hold time is the minimum time data must remain stable after the clock edge so that the capture completes. A concrete example: a typical FPGA flip-flop might have T_co around 0.2 nanoseconds and T_setup around 0.1 nanoseconds; both are small but non-zero contributors to the path delay. Misunderstandings often arise when designers assume hold checks are unnecessary; while hold violations are less common in FPGAs due to routing delays, they can occur with negative skew or very short routing between registers. Consider a design that launches data and the capture register is physically close; the data could arrive so quickly that it violates the hold requirement. The practical response is to add small routing delay or use tool features to adjust hold timing, not to ignore the problem. When reasoning about pipelining, remember that adding registers reduces T_logic for each stage but adds one T_co and one T_setup per stage in the timing equation. The decision to pipeline balances maximum frequency against increased latency, and a real design example will reveal whether that trade-off is acceptable.

keyIdea.title: Flip-flop timing
keyIdea.text: T_co, T_setup, and hold time are small constants that critically affect whether a path meets timing at high frequencies.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Flip-Flop Timing
Terms defined
  • T_co: clock-to-Q delay; time until output is stable after the clock edge.
  • T_setup: data must be stable this long before the capture edge.
  • Hold time: data must remain stable after the edge to be captured correctly.
Example numbers commonly used in illustrations: T_co ≈ 0.2 ns, T_setup ≈ 0.1 ns. These are not zero and contribute to the required clock period.
Concrete scenario
If a launching flip-flop has T_co of 0.2 ns and the path through logic takes 6 ns, and the receiving register needs 0.1 ns setup, the required time without skew is 6.3 ns. If you target 10 ns clock period, slack is 3.7 ns.
Common pitfall
Hold violation

Do not assume hold violations can't happen. They can occur with small routing delay or negative skew; inspect hold checks if you see unstable capturing behavior.

Pro tip
When pipelining, add registers where T_logic dominates to reduce stage delay and increase f_max.
Why it matters
Small timing parameters limit top-end clock frequency; they compound with logic delays on each path.
Check
Always include vendor flip-flop timing in STA runs; don't assume idealized zero delays.

screens.title: Setup vs. Hold Violations
screens.subtitle: What they look like and how to fix them

narration.text: Setup and hold violations are two distinct timing failures with different root causes and fixes. A setup violation occurs when the data arrives too late to meet the required setup window before the clock edge. This happens when the sum of clock-to-Q, logic delay, setup time, and skew exceeds the clock period. Practically, it's the symptom you get when the critical path is too long for your target frequency. The remedy is to reduce the path delay: simplify logic, use faster resources, shorten routing, or add pipeline registers. In contrast, a hold violation happens when data arrives too early after the clock edge and changes before the capture completes. Hold issues are often caused by very short routing delays, negative skew, or asynchronous interactions. The fix can be to add small routing delay, enable hold buffers provided by the tool, or insert local registers where appropriate. A common misconception is that the same fix applies to both; it does not. Pipelining reduces setup pressure but can increase hold risk for neighboring paths, so always re-run STA after changes. A concrete example: in our 4-bit ALU, adding a pipeline register in the middle halves T_logic for each stage, resolving setup violations at higher clock rates while adding one cycle of latency. The closing question: when you add a register to fix setup, where might hold problems appear and how would you detect them in reports?

keyIdea.title: Different failures, different fixes
keyIdea.text: Setup violations need longer clock period or less logic; hold violations need added delay or local buffering.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Setup vs Hold
Setup violation
Definition: Data arrives after the required setup window and cannot be captured correctly at the clock edge.
Fixes
  • Add pipeline register to shorten logic per stage.
  • Optimize combinational logic or routing.
  • Reduce clock frequency if necessary.
Hold violation
Definition: New data changes too quickly after the clock edge and corrupts capture of the old data.
Fixes
  • Add small routing delay or use hold buffers.
  • Avoid negative skew that makes launch earlier than capture.
  • Insert local registers where appropriate.
Concrete example
Pipelining a long ALU path halves logic delay per stage and resolves setup failures at higher clock rates, but the added register introduces new neighbor paths to check for hold.
Pro tip
After any timing change, re-run both setup and hold analysis; they catch different problems.
Check
Use the timing report to find negative slack for setup and unusual early arrivals for hold violations.

screens.title: Clock skew and uncertainty
screens.subtitle: How clock distribution affects available timing window

narration.text: Clock skew is the difference in arrival time of the clock edge at different flip-flops and it directly affects timing margins. Skew can be positive or negative: positive skew reduces available time for a given path because the capture clock arrives later, while negative skew can sometimes help a particular path but may hurt others. Clock uncertainty, which you express with set_clock_uncertainty, models jitter and other non-deterministic effects and is often added to the required time as an extra margin. Together, skew and uncertainty are safety buffers the STA must consider. A concrete example: adding a 0.2 nanosecond clock uncertainty with a 0.5 nanosecond measured skew increases the required window and therefore reduces slack. Misconceptions include thinking skew only matters for long paths; in reality, even short paths can fail if skew or uncertainty shift the window enough. Practically, you can reduce skew by improving clock distribution or by constraining placement and routing for clock nets, but you must balance the trade-offs in an FPGA where the vendor clock network is often pre-built. The closing takeaway: include realistic skew and uncertainty in your constraints so the reported slack reflects real-life timing margins and not an optimistic ideal.

keyIdea.title: Skew and uncertainty
keyIdea.text: Clock skew and uncertainty shrink the available timing window; include them in constraints to avoid optimistic slack.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Clock Skew
What is clock skew?
The difference in clock edge arrival times between registers due to routing or distribution network variation.
Effects
  • Positive skew reduces available time, hurting setup checks.
  • Negative skew can reduce hold margin, creating hold risks.
Clock uncertainty
Timing jitter and other non-deterministic effects modeled with set_clock_uncertainty to add margin to setup checks.
Example

Using set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.200 models 0.2 ns uncertainty that reduces reported slack and encourages safer timing decisions.

Pro tip
Include clock uncertainty conservatively early, then tune once silicon or implementation timing is measured.
Why it matters
Without skew and uncertainty, timing reports can be overly optimistic and miss real failures.
Check
If slack is marginal, inspect skew values in the timing report before deciding on fixes.

screens.title: Writing SDC: create_clock and uncertainty
screens.subtitle: Essential clock constraint commands in SDC

narration.text: The create_clock command is the most important SDC instruction because it tells the timing tool the clock name, the period, and where the clock is driven. A common form used in Quartus or Vivado is create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 [get_ports {clk}], which defines a 50 megahertz clock on the port named clk. You can specify a waveform with the open and close times, for example waveform {0.000 10.000} to indicate a 50% duty cycle. After creating the clock, you often want to model uncertainty with set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.200 [get_clocks {clk}] so the analyzer reduces the available time for setup checks by that amount. A concrete tip: always place clock creation and uncertainty at the top of your. sdc so the analyzer knows the domain before examining input/output or path constraints. A misconception to avoid is forgetting to attach create_clock to the pin or net that actually drives the design; if the tool doesn't find the clock source, it cannot analyze the domain. In practice, verify that [get_ports {clk}] or the clock net matches your design's naming. The closing question: after adding create_clock and uncertainty, how will reported slack change and why? You will see slack reduced by the uncertainty amount in worst-case checks.

keyIdea.title: create_clock
keyIdea.text: create_clock defines the clock period and is required for meaningful STA; follow it with uncertainty when modeling jitter.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › SDC: create_clock
SDC example
create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 [get_ports {clk}]
create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 -waveform {0.000 10.000} [get_ports {clk}]
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.200 [get_clocks {clk}]
Place these lines at the top of your .sdc so the analyzer knows the clock domain before other constraints.
Concrete advice
If the tool cannot resolve the clock source name exactly, it will not analyze that domain. Match port or net names precisely, and prefer explicit waveform and uncertainty when jitter or duty cycle matters.
Key Takeaway

Define clocks and their uncertainty first so other SDC directives are interpreted relative to known domains.

Misconception
Omitting uncertainty makes reports optimistic; always model expected jitter conservatively.
Check
Verify the clock name resolves with get_clocks in the tool before running full timing analysis.
Why it matters
Timing decisions depend on the clock period and uncertainty; these drive whether slack is positive or negative.

screens.title: I/O Delays: set_input_delay and set_output_delay
screens.subtitle: How external timing affects internal timing budgets

narration.text: Input and output delays communicate external device timing to the STA so it can allocate internal slack correctly. The set_input_delay command tells the analyzer when valid data arrives at an input port relative to a clock edge. For example, set_input_delay -clock {clk} -max 5.000 [get_ports {data_in}] means an external driver will present valid data at most 5 nanoseconds after the referenced clock edge. Conversely, set_input_delay -min specifies the earliest arrival for hold analysis. Output delays are symmetric: set_output_delay -clock {clk} -max 3.000 [get_ports {data_out}] tells the analyzer the external receiver needs the output to be stable at least 3 nanoseconds before the next clock edge. A concrete example: if an ADC drives your FPGA and the ADC’s data is valid only 4 ns after the clock, you must express that with set_input_delay so the tool does not artificially assume zero external latency. A common misconception is to provide only max delays and ignore min delays; that can cause incorrect hold analysis because the min timing sets the earliest possible arrival. Always supply both -max and -min when you can. The practical step is to record the external device datasheet timings and translate them into set_input_delay and set_output_delay entries in the. sdc. After adding these, re-run timing to see how the internal slack shifts to accommodate the input and output requirements.

keyIdea.title: I/O constraints
keyIdea.text: Input/output delays tell STA when external data is valid so the analyzer can compute realistic internal slack.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › I/O Delays
Input delay example
set_input_delay -clock {clk} -max 5.000 [get_ports {data_in}]
set_input_delay -clock {clk} -min 1.000 [get_ports {data_in}]
Max models latest valid arrival for setup; min models earliest arrival for hold analysis.
Output delay example
set_output_delay -clock {clk} -max 3.000 [get_ports {data_out}]
Models the time the external device needs the data before its next clock edge.
Concrete scenario
An ADC that updates 4 ns after the clock implies set_input_delay -max 4.0 so your FPGA sampling logic meets the real-world arrival.
Misconception
Assuming zero external delay makes internal timing appear easier than it is; always model I/O.
Check
Use datasheet numbers for external devices to populate -max and -min I/O delays accurately.

screens.title: False paths and Multicycle paths
screens.subtitle: When to tell the analyzer to ignore or relax paths

narration.text: Sometimes paths should not be treated as single-cycle timing-critical connections. False paths are those that will never be exercised in normal operation — for example, a reset path that is only active at power-up or a path gated by mutually exclusive control signals. You tell the analyzer to ignore them with set_false_path so STA does not waste effort or report meaningless violations. Multicycle paths are paths where the design intentionally allows data to take multiple clock cycles to travel from launch to capture, such as a slow divider output. Use set_multicycle_path to relax the analyzer by specifying the number of cycles the path may consume. A concrete example: if a slow peripheral updates every three clocks, set_multicycle_path -from [get_registers launch] -to [get_registers capture] -setup 3 tells STA the path is allowed three cycles instead of one. A typical misconception is to overuse false-path or multicycle annotations to hide failures; annotations must reflect real design intent and be documented. Incorrect use can mask genuine timing bugs. The practical workflow is to identify candidate paths in timing reports, confirm via logic review that they are indeed false or multicycle, then add explicit SDC lines and re-run STA. Always re-check the reports after annotations to ensure no unexpected side-effects.

keyIdea.title: Path annotations
keyIdea.text: Use set_false_path and set_multicycle_path to express design intent; annotate only when logically justified.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › False & Multicycle Paths
False path
A path that is logically unreachable during normal operation. Example: a reset-only connection that is never toggled in regular runs.
set_false_path -from [get_ports {reset}] -to [get_registers *]
Multicycle path
A path intentionally taking more than one clock cycle to transfer valid data. Example: a slow control signal updated every 3 cycles.
set_multicycle_path -from [get_regs launch] -to [get_regs capture] -setup 3
Concrete advice
Annotate only after confirming logic-level exclusivity or intentional multicycle timing; document each annotation.
Misconception
Annotations are not a substitute for fixing real timing issues; they must reflect implementation intent.
Check
After adding an annotation, re-run STA and confirm no hidden negative slack remains in unrelated domains.

screens.title: Slack and Critical Path Analysis in TimeQuest
screens.subtitle: How to read the Setup Summary and target fixes

narration.text: Timing tools like TimeQuest produce a Setup Summary that lists worst-case slack for each clock domain and reports the critical path when slack is negative. Slack is defined as Data Required Time minus Data Arrival Time. A positive slack means the design meets timing; negative slack is a failure that points to a specific critical path. The critical path lists the launching register, every logic element and routing delay, and the capture register at the end. A concrete workflow: run a full compilation, open TimeQuest, view the Setup Summary to find the worst slack, then inspect the critical path listed for that slack. The path will show which LUTs or carry chains dominate delay and whether routing contributes significantly. A common misconception is to trust only the slack number; instead, always inspect the node-by-node breakdown in the report to identify actionable optimizations. For example, if routing delay dominates, placement constraints or floorplanning may help; if LUT depth dominates, restructure the logic or pipeline it. The closing question for practice: when you see a critical path dominated by carry chains, what are your optimization options and which change is least invasive?

keyIdea.title: From slack to fix
keyIdea.text: Use the Setup Summary to find worst slack and inspect the critical path to choose targeted fixes like pipelining or placement changes.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Slack & Critical Path
Interpreting slack
Slack = Data Required Time − Data Arrival Time. Positive slack passes; negative slack fails and points to a critical path.
Practical steps
  1. Run compile and STA.
  2. Open Setup Summary to find worst slack.
  3. Inspect critical path node-by-node to find dominant delays.
Concrete actions
If logic delay dominates, refactor or pipeline. If routing dominates, apply placement or floorplan constraints. If skew/uncertainty dominates, adjust clocking or constraints.
Key Takeaway

Critical path analysis points to the exact nodes to optimize; use it to choose targeted fixes rather than blind changes.

Misconception
Believing slack alone is enough; node-level analysis is required to decide fixes.
Pro tip
Use the timing report's node breakdown to compare logic delay vs routing delay contributions.
Check
After applying a fix, re-run STA to see whether slack improved and whether new critical paths appeared.

screens.title: Practical: 4-bit ALU timing and pipelining
screens.subtitle: Add an .sdc, run TimeQuest, then pipeline to improve f_max

narration.text: This hands-on sequence walks through the exercise described in the chapter. Start with the 4-bit ALU RTL and add a. sdc containing a create_clock line for a 50 megahertz target: create_clock -name {clk} -period 20.000 [get_ports {clk}]. Add set_input_delay and set_output_delay for external pins if the board peripherals specify them. Compile the design and run TimeQuest Timing Analyzer, then open the Setup Summary to identify the worst slack and the critical path. You will usually see a long combinational path across ALU logic and carry chains as the critical path. Next, increase the clock frequency target to 100 megahertz by changing the period to 10.000 and re-run the flow. Observe how slack decreases or becomes negative; the critical path will be the same physical path but now exceeds the shorter period. To fix this, add a pipeline register that splits the combinational path into two stages. After pipelining, re-run compilation and timing: you should see the combinational delay per stage roughly halve, improving maximum achievable frequency at the cost of one extra clock cycle of latency. A common pitfall is to forget to update or add appropriate multicycle or false-path constraints when changing the design; re-check input and output delays and hold checks after pipelining. The exercise demonstrates the practical trade-offs between throughput and latency and teaches how to iterate on timing-driven RTL changes.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline trade-off
keyIdea.text: Adding registers splits long paths to raise f_max but increases latency and requires re-running STA for both setup and hold.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › ALU Lab
Step-by-step
  1. Create .sdc: add create_clock for 50 MHz and I/O delays.
  2. Compile and run TimeQuest; open Setup Summary to find worst slack and critical path.
  3. Change clock period to 10 ns for 100 MHz and re-run; observe slack change.
  4. Add a pipeline register to split combinational logic and re-run timing.
  5. Compare critical path delay and acknowledge throughput vs latency trade-off.
Concrete numbers
If initial path has T_co = 0.3 ns, T_logic = 12 ns, T_setup = 0.2 ns, T_skew = 0.5 ns, minimum clock period is 13.0 ns (≈76.9 MHz). Splitting logic into two stages halves T_logic to 6 ns per stage and yields 7.0 ns period (≈142.9 MHz), doubling throughput but adding latency.
Key Takeaway

Use STA-driven iterations: constrain, run, inspect critical path, and modify RTL based on report data instead of guessing.

Misconception
Pipelining always solves timing without cost. It increases latency and may introduce hold cases to check.
Pro tip
Document each .sdc change and the reason for adding annotations, so future reviewers understand intent.
Check
After changes, re-run both setup and hold STA to confirm no new violations exist.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the core concepts to retain. First, STA is exhaustive and complementary to dynamic simulation; it identifies worst-case timing paths that functionally correct testbenches may miss. Second, the timing equation T_clock ≥ T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew governs whether a synchronous path meets setup; slack quantifies the margin. Third, SDC constraints such as create_clock, set_input_delay, and set_output_delay communicate clock and input and output timing to the analyzer and are required for meaningful reports. Fourth, false paths and multicycle paths must be annotated when the design intent allows them; annotations should reflect logic behavior, not hide failures. Fifth, TimeQuest and Vivado provide Setup Summary and critical path detail — use node-by-node analysis to decide between pipelining, logic optimization, or placement fixes. Keep these concepts in mind as you translate RTL into timing-clean FPGA implementations.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: STA, the timing equation, SDC constraints, path annotations, and critical path analysis form the closed loop for timing closure.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Key Concepts
STA is exhaustive
Mathematically checks all paths; use it with simulation for correctness plus timing safety.
Timing equation
T_clock ≥ T_co + T_logic + T_setup + T_skew; slack measures margin.
SDC constraints
create_clock, set_input_delay, set_output_delay, set_false_path, set_multicycle_path.
Summary takeaway: express realistic clocks and I/O timing, run STA, inspect slack and critical paths, then iterate on RTL or constraints until timing is clean.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for practical timing work

narration.text: Keep these three compact reminders in your toolkit. First, always define clocks and uncertainties up front in an. sdc so the timing tool analyzes meaningful domains. Second, use input and output delays to model real external device timing; missing input and output delays gives unrealistic slack. Third, when a critical path fails, inspect its node-level breakdown in the timing report and choose an informed fix: pipeline to split logic, optimize logic to reduce LUT depth, or constrain placement to reduce routing. These steps form a repeatable pattern: constrain, analyze, inspect, and modify. Regularly re-run both setup and hold analysis after changes to avoid surprises. Quick Reference means define clocks, model i/o, inspect critical path details, and iterate with sta-driven rtl changes.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for practical timing work. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical checklist
keyIdea.text: Define clocks, model I/O, inspect critical path details, and iterate with STA-driven RTL changes.

content.html:

Define clocks first
create_clock and uncertainty belong at the top of your .sdc.
Model I/O
Use set_input_delay and set_output_delay from datasheet values for realistic STA.
Inspect critical path
Use the node-by-node report to choose targeted fixes like pipelining or placement changes.
Keep this checklist on hand when preparing FPGA constraints and running TimeQuest or Vivado: it prevents optimistic timing assumptions and guides practical fixes.
